newsitem.title: USA: Republicans skeptical about childrens' health bills.
newsitem.headline: Republicans skeptical about childrens' health bills.

text.p: House Republicans on Tuesday gingerly entered the growing debate over providing health care to the country's 10 million uninsured children, questioning just what, if anything, Congress should do.

At their first hearing on the issue, Republicans were uncertain whether childrens' insurance should be a priority. Experts told lawmakers that setting up new federal subsidies could create a financial incentive for workers and employers to drop private health coverage in favour of government aid.

"So far, the issue has generated significantly more interest than solutions," California Republican Representative Bill Thomas told a House Ways and Means subcommittee hearing. "The facts about uninsured children are much more complex than many have appreciated or understood."
At the same time, across the Capitol, an unlikely bipartisan duo formally introduced a bill to give states $20 billion over five years to design and run children's health programmes.
The legislation by Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy and Utah Republican Sen. Orrin Hatch would be funded by nearly tripling the federal cigarette tax to 67 cents a pack.

The senators first unveiled the plan last month. Their efforts have picked up some steam, including the support of Vermont Republican Sen. Jim Jeffords, chair of the committee that oversees the issue. But Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott does not support the tobacco tax increase.
The number of uninsured children under age 18 has grown to 10 million in recent years, in part due to cutbacks in coverage offered by private insurance companies."
Congressional Democrats have made childrens' care their No. 1 health priority for this session of Congress, introducing bills to provide tax credits and subsidies for coverage.
President Bill Clinton's balanced budget plan calls for expanding coverage to as many as 5 million children, mainly by boosting enrollment in the Medicaid programme for the poor.
Underscoring the political stakes, House Democrats on Tuesday asked Thomas to schedule a committee vote on childrens' health by Mother's Day, May 11, and a House vote by Father's Day, June 15.
"Congress has a responsibility to address the epidemic of uninsured children," the Democrats said in a letter.
House Republicans have been struggling to figure out how to respond on the issue, saying they want a free-market solution rather than a government-mandated approach.
Private health experts suggested on Tuesday that the government first focus on expanding coverage to the 3 million children who are eligible for Medicaid but are not enrolled.
They warned that some people might shift to government aid from private insurance, while businesses could stop providing coverage if a new government programme were created.

"Reducing the number of uninsured children significantly would require generous levels of direct subsidies or tax credits and it would be difficult to prevent low-income children who would otherwise have private coverage from participating in such a generous programme," said Linda Bilheimer of the Congressional Budget Office.

Some Republicans suggested greater use of community health clinics or broader state efforts. They also suggested requiring low-income people to buy insurance for their children as a condition for receiving current federal tax breaks.
